title: New Housing Fund Rules: Take What You Can, But Don't Treat It as a Savings Account
dek: The housing provident fund is not a savings account you can withdraw at will — fraudulent withdrawals are prosecuted and bar you from any withdrawal for three years. But the new rules put renting first in the withdrawal order and scrap the rent-to-income ratio cap, so money you should take is still money you should take.
why: Three people in different situations — a self-employed worker, a young professional, a property owner — each run their own numbers, turning the 20 clause changes in the new rules into concrete decisions. The second half, on flexible-employment contributions and the comparison with the public sector, is especially informative.
who: Employees who have a provident fund but aren't sure whether to withdraw or leave it; people considering buying a home, converting a commercial loan to a provident fund loan, or contributing as flexible-employment workers; job seekers trying to judge whether a company is well-run.
skip: The opening chat about how the episode came about and the three hosts' positions can be fast-forwarded; start at 13:10, where Zhou Yi's experience of using hers begins.

points.h: Six months after auto-withdrawal, I paused it myself
points.body: After Zhou Yi turned on Beijing's no-threshold monthly rent withdrawal of 2,000 yuan, she found the money slid into another card the moment it arrived, completely decoupled from the mental account for paying rent; when her spending card ran out at month's end, the money was auto-deducted, which only added friction to daily life. Once she confirmed the fund balance earns 1.5% interest, higher than the roughly 0.95% on a one-year bank time deposit, she paused the withdrawal the next day. Yubai notes this contrasts with the advice three years ago to ‘take everything you can and use everything you can’, and two young colleagues in the department have made the same choice. Lao Qian cautions that this is indeed a low-efficiency use of funds, but most people can't achieve the efficiency they imagine — people just keep fake books for themselves.

points.h: The fund is not a deposit; not being able to take it out is the norm
points.body: Yubai walks through an extreme case: a young person loses their job and goes home with no liquid funds, tens of thousands of yuan sitting in the provident fund, but the home is owner-occupied, so it qualifies neither as a home purchase nor as renting; even if the new rules allow withdrawal under the headings of renovation or property fees, if the family has no such needs there is nothing to be done. If you risk it and fabricate a purpose to withdraw fraudulently, you must return the entire amount and cannot withdraw any provident fund for three years. So both approaches hold — ‘take everything you can’ and ‘treat it as forced savings at a rate above demand deposits’ — and it comes down to the individual case.

points.h: The new rules put renting first in the withdrawal order
points.body: This revision adjusts 20 clauses in total. First, renovating an owner-occupied home and paying property fees on an owner-occupied home are included as withdrawal purposes for the first time; the fund no longer serves only loan-financed home purchases. Second, renting used to require that rent exceed a set proportion of household wage income; this version removes that restriction, and renting is placed first in the withdrawal order. Third, flexible-employment workers are formally brought into the system for the first time: self-employed individuals and part-time workers may contribute voluntarily and apply for provident fund loans. In addition, the management centre must reply to withdrawal applications within three days and to loan applications within ten days, and nationwide mutual recognition of contribution records is being pushed forward.

points.h: The share of contributions lent out has fallen from 70% to 30%
points.body: The figure Lao Qian saw: this year the proportion of provident fund contributions lent out is as low as just over 30%, against more than 70% at the peak — a steady decline in just a few years. In other words, the theoretically most stable, lowest-rate, highest-quality lending channel is actually used by only a bit over 30% of people. That directly reflects how low the willingness to buy is. Lao Qian also points out the new rules aim at housing consumption rather than leverage: renting moved to first place, property fees and renovation both withdrawable, thresholds sharply lowered — supporting measures as the property market shifts from an incremental to a stock phase, and also echoing the ageing trend: the month when the withdrawal ratio turned up was 2023, exactly when the post-1960 cohort retired.

points.h: If you want to buy, be careful about withdrawing
points.body: Yubai warns: the provident fund loan amount is tied to the account balance — in some cities you can borrow 16 times the balance, in others 20 times, varying by city. Guangzhou has several caps, and at application the smallest of the standards applies: for a first or second owner-occupied home the minimum down payment is 20%, so on a 1 million yuan home the loan cannot exceed 800,000; and a monthly repayment exceeding 50% of monthly income also fails. So before taking the fund out as living expenses, check your city's lending rules. Yubai is also cautious about the buying logic of ‘rent-to-price ratio close to the provident fund rate, only a down payment short’: you still have to weigh depreciation, price swings, and how to withstand risk once a 600,000 down payment is locked up.

points.h: Flexible-employment contributors carry the full amount alone
points.body: For flexible-employment workers the contribution base and rate are calculated the same way as for employees, but no employer pays half, so one person bears the full 10% to 24%. The base must be self-declared: below 10,000 no proof is needed, above 10,000 you must log into the individual income tax app and pull your tax details as documentation, to prevent inflating the base to extract a higher loan amount. Zhou Yi ran the numbers: 10,000 at 10% to 24% is 1,000 to 2,400 yuan, and this money is not counted in individual income tax, but it is a loss if you never use it. In addition, most pilot cities require 6 to 12 consecutive months of contributions before you can apply for a provident fund loan, and most do not allow one-off back payments.

points.h: In the public sector the fund is an invisible benefit
points.body: Zhou Yi asked a friend with a public-institution post back home, who readily showed a screenshot of her provident fund account: the monthly credit is more than twice Zhou Yi's, and the balance already exceeds her savings. The friend lives at home with no need to rent, so the fund just accumulates as forced savings or future loan capacity, plus she has an occupational annuity, and the contribution base counts bonuses and allowances in full. Lao Qian adds: the provident fund is tax-free, and with private pensions capped at 12,000 yuan a year and taxed at 3% on withdrawal, the public sector already has an extra layer of tax advantage. On the data: in 2025 the average annual wage of urban non-private unit employees nationwide was 129,441 yuan, against 71,590 yuan for private units — while working hours run the other way.

points.h: Full provident fund contributions are a slice for judging a company
points.body: Lao Qian's judgment on ‘is a company that pays the provident fund a better choice’ has not changed at all: a company that contributes in full respects its employees and respects the rules, which means it is probably well-run in every respect, rather than finding workarounds for every policy. He goes further: this points to not making profit maximisation the first goal, to treating people as people, and the invisible returns show up elsewhere. Zhou Yi has run the numbers: on a wage base of 100, you actually take home just over 70, but the boss pays out over 130, and everyone along the chain feels aggrieved. Lao Qian cites Ford's pay raise on the Model T — letting workers afford a car and have time to use it was not the capitalist having a conscience, it was simply a better utility function.

quotes.text: It arrives, but because your phone gets so many app notifications you don't look carefully — say it tells you 2,000 yuan came in, and it just sits in that card until the end of the month, when my spending card is used up and it gets auto-deducted from that card.
But the fact is people keep fake books for themselves, people withdraw on the spot for all sorts of reasons, people are very good at deceiving themselves.
You really can't treat the provident fund as a deposit, because your bank deposit you can take out at any time, but the provident fund you can't.
And it's the highest-quality lending channel, the rate is so low, yet only a bit over 30% of people took out a loan — and at the peak, what was that proportion? Over 70% — in just a few years.
I think a company that contributes the provident fund in full shows it respects its employees and respects the rules.

Treating people as people doesn't mean raising costs; it also means one person's spending, the household sector's spending, becomes the corporate sector's income, and the corporate sector's spending becomes the household sector's wages — the two form a virtuous cycle.
Take everything you can and use everything you can — buying a home, building, renovating, repaying a loan, renting, retirement, leaving the country, all of it can be used.
